from.place: Free dg-category presentations, finite presentability and word filtrations used to construct the quasi-equivalence model and local cofibrancy, in the finite mapping-complex adjunction of proof paragraph 2.

title: Free dg-category presentations and arrow-word filtrations
statement:
Fix universes as in [def-weil-size-convention] and a commutative ring $R$ in the small universe $\mathcal U$. A cochain complex of $R$-modules is a $\mathbf Z$-graded module with a differential $d$ of degree $1$ satisfying $d^2=0$. An $R$-linear dg category has a $\mathcal U$-small object set, cochain complexes of $\mathcal U$-small $R$-modules as morphisms, associative unital compositions, and the signed Leibniz rule $d(ba)=d(b)a+(-1)^{|b|}b\,d(a)$; dg functors preserve this data. The category $\operatorname{dgcat}_R$ of these categories and dg functors has $\mathcal U$-small Hom sets, all $\mathcal U$-small limits and colimits, and is locally finitely presentable: a $\mathcal U$-small set of finitely presentable objects generates it under filtered colimits. Here filtered means that every finite diagram admits a cocone, and finitely presentable means that the object's Hom functor preserves filtered colimits. Finite dg presentations (finitely many objects and homogeneous arrows, with differentials specified by finite words, and finitely many relations compatible with the differential) are finitely presentable. Filtered colimits have the filtered colimit object set and, for any pair of objects represented at a common stage, the filtered colimit morphism complex over later stages. More precisely, for a filtered diagram indexed by $I$ and $x_i,y_i$ at stage $i$, this morphism complex is $\varinjlim_{(u:i\to j)\in i/I}\mathcal C_j(u x_i,u y_i)$.

Let $\mathbf1_R$ be the one-object dg category with endomorphisms $R$ in degree zero. For a complex $V$ let $T(V)$ have objects $0,1$, endomorphisms $R$, morphisms $T(V)(1,0)=0$, and $T(V)(0,1)=V$. Dg functors $T(V)\to\mathcal C$ are naturally pairs of objects $s,t$ of $\mathcal C$ and chain maps $V\to\mathcal C(s,t)$. In particular all $T(V)$ for finitely presented complexes $V$ (meaning that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Ch}(R)}(V,-)$ preserves filtered colimits) are finitely presentable. Adjoining freely a homogeneous arrow $e:s\to t$ of degree $n$ to $\mathcal C$, with $d(e)=a$ for a prescribed closed $a\in\mathcal C(s,t)^{n+1}$, leaves its object set unchanged. Its morphism complex from $x$ to $y$ has an exhaustive increasing filtration $F_m$ by the number of occurrences of $e$. Its $F_0$ is $\mathcal C(x,y)$, all filtration inclusions split as graded $R$-modules, and for $m\geq1$ its quotient is
$$F_m/F_{m-1}\cong\mathcal C(t,y)\otimes_R Re\otimes_R\bigl(\mathcal C(t,s)\otimes_R Re\bigr)^{\otimes_R(m-1)}\otimes_R\mathcal C(x,s),$$
where $Re$ is $R$ in degree $n$ with zero differential. The differential on words is the Leibniz differential and the terms involving $d(e)=a$ lower word length. If instead a whole complex $V$ of arrows $s\to t$ is freely adjoined with its own differential, the morphism complex is the direct sum of the length-zero summand $\mathcal C(x,y)$ and these same word terms with $Re$ replaced by $V$, with the tensor differential on each summand. These descriptions and filtrations are natural in the attaching data. Tensor products of modules in these formulas are those of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], with graded tensor degree given by the sum of the factor degrees.

source.place: Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, generators and Lemma 1.10 word construction and smallness, printed pp. 28-30. Finite-presentation/filtered-colimit formulation and arbitrary arrow-degree generalization by the agent. Read online; not locally archived. No corresponding Stacks tag.

proof.text: Use the size convention of [def-weil-size-convention]. Here is an explicit finite-limit sketch in the sense defined in [lem-coef-finite-limit-sketch-models]. Take sorts $O$ and $A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbf Z$, maps $s_n,t_n:A_n\to O$, and the finite pullback sorts for parallel arrows, composable pairs, and the triples needed in the laws. Include maps $z_n:O\times O\to A_n$, scalar multiplications $A_n\to A_n$ for each $r\in R$, negation, addition on parallel pairs, identities $O\to A_0$, compositions $A_q\times_O A_p\to A_{p+q}$, and $d_n:A_n\to A_{n+1}$. Impose the source-target equations, the $R$-module equations in each fiber of $(s_n,t_n)$, associativity, units and bilinearity of composition, linearity of $d$, $d(1)=0$, $d_{n+1}d_n=z_{n+2}(s_n,t_n)$, and the stated signed Leibniz equation on each composable-pair sort. Equations are equalities of maps, hence relations in the indexing category. Every tuple of maps into the vertex of a specified cone that an equation uses (for example $(r\circ\mathrm{pr}_1,r\circ\mathrm{pr}_2)$ on the parallel-pair sort, or the pairs of $d\circ\mathrm{pr}_1,\mathrm{pr}_2$ and $\mathrm{pr}_1,d\circ\mathrm{pr}_2$ on a composable-pair sort in the Leibniz equation) is included as a generating arrow into that vertex, with the equations prescribing its composites with the cone projections; since a model sends the cone to a limit, such an arrow is sent to the induced pairing, and a dg category determines it uniquely; the only specified limit cones are finite products and pullbacks. The free category on this signature modulo these equations is small: there are only $\mathcal U$-many sorts, operations, finite strings and equations. A model gives exactly a dg category by setting $\mathcal C(x,y)^n=(s_n,t_n)^{-1}(x,y)$; the inverse construction takes $A_n$ to the disjoint union of these fibers. Transformations give exactly dg functors, including arbitrary object maps. These two constructions are mutually inverse up to the evident natural identifications.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-finite-limit-sketch-models] to this small finite-limit sketch. Its conclusion gives small Hom sets, all small limits and colimits, and a small filtered generating family of finitely presentable objects. The identification in step 1 preserves functors, so these are assertions about ordinary strict $R$-linear dg categories and dg functors; no localization, equivalence of object spaces, or homotopy colimit is being substituted. It also says that the object sort and every homogeneous-arrow sort of a filtered colimit are their colimits of sets.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 28-30; explicit agent generalization and verification, not a locally archived proof.

proof.text: For completeness identify the fixed-endpoint fibers of that filtered colimit. Write $\mathcal C=\varinjlim_I\mathcal C_i$ and fix $x_i,y_i$. The category $i/I$ of arrows out of $i$ is nonempty and filtered: first choose a common target of a finite list of targets, then equalize the resulting finite list of parallel arrows out of $i$. By the pointwise filtered-colimit clause of [lem-coef-finite-limit-sketch-models] and the representative/equality clauses of [lem-weil-pbc-filtered-colimit-sets-elementwise], every degree-$n$ arrow of $\mathcal C$ between the images of $x_i,y_i$ has a representative at some stage; pass to a common target with $i$ and then impose the two endpoint equalities at a later stage. It therefore comes from $\mathcal C_j(u x_i,u y_i)^n$. If two such representatives have equal images, the same equality clause makes them equal at a common target; equalize the two induced maps from $i$ to that target as well. This proves bijectivity of the map from the colimit over $i/I$. Addition, scalars and differential are represented at common stages, so the bijections are an isomorphism of complexes. For objects initially represented at different stages first take a common target. This proves the asserted meaning of 'later stages' even when $I$ has parallel morphisms.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 28-30; explicit agent generalization and verification, not a locally archived proof.

proof.text: Let $P$ have a finite dg presentation. A map $P\to\mathcal C$ is precisely a choice of images of its finitely many objects and homogeneous-arrow generators, subject to the finitely many specified relations and the finitely many equations $d(g)=q_g$, where each $q_g$ is a finite linear combination of composable words. There are no extra checks for all words: a generator assignment satisfying these equations extends by composition and linearity, and Leibniz extends commutation with $d$ to each word; relations and their differentials then vanish. In a filtered colimit all these finitely many chosen images are represented together, by [lem-weil-pbc-filtered-colimit-sets-elementwise] and filteredness. Their finitely many endpoint, differential and relation equations hold together at a later stage, by that node's equality criterion applied successively. This factors the map through some $\mathcal C_j$. If two stage maps become equal, apply the same criterion to their finitely many object and arrow images; equality on generators is equality of dg functors. Thus the canonical map from the filtered colimit of Hom sets is both surjective and injective. This proves finite presentability of every stated finite dg presentation, without assuming that its morphism modules are finitely generated.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 28-30; explicit agent generalization and verification, not a locally archived proof.

proof.text: In $T(V)$ the only non-scalar morphisms are those of $V$ from $0$ to $1$. There is no composable pair of such arrows, so its compositions are scalar actions and the scalar units, and its differential is $d_V$ and zero on $R$. The dg identities follow from linearity of $d_V$. A dg functor chooses $s,t$ and one chain map $V\to\mathcal C(s,t)$; conversely these data uniquely give a functor since its maps on both copies of $R$ must send $r$ to $r1$. This includes $s=t$, and proves the natural classification. The category $\mathbf1_R$ is defined by the same scalar unit and multiplication.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 28-30; explicit agent generalization and verification, not a locally archived proof.

proof.text: Suppose $V$ is finitely presentable in $\operatorname{Ch}(R)$ in the sense specified in the statement. A functor $T(V)\to\varinjlim_I\mathcal C_i$ first chooses two objects; represent them at a common stage $i$. By step 3 its chain map has target $\varinjlim_{i/I}\mathcal C_j(u s,u t)$. Finite presentability of $V$ factors it through one term. For two functors with equal colimit images, the object equality criterion of [lem-weil-pbc-filtered-colimit-sets-elementwise] first makes their two object images equal at a common stage; finite presentability of $V$ applied to the subsequent $i/I$ diagram makes their chain maps equal after a further transition. This is exactly the injectivity, as well as surjectivity, of the map of Hom sets. Thus $T(V)$ is finitely presentable, including $V=0$. No termwise finite-presentation assumption on an unbounded complex is used.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 28-30; explicit agent generalization and verification, not a locally archived proof.

proof.text: We now construct the graded normal form instead of inferring it from a pushout theorem. Let $E$ be a graded $R$-module of arrows $s\to t$, with no differential yet. For $m\geq1$ put $W_m(x,y)=\mathcal C(t,y)\otimes E\otimes(\mathcal C(t,s)\otimes E)^{\otimes(m-1)}\otimes\mathcal C(x,s)$ as a graded module and put $W_0(x,y)=\mathcal C(x,y)$. Tensor products mean degreewise tensors followed by the direct sum over degree tuples of prescribed total degree. Use the tensor-product universal property and pure-tensor generation of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The graded module $W(x,y)=\bigoplus_{m\geq0}W_m(x,y)$ consists of finite sums of tensors $b_m v_m b_{m-1}\cdots v_1 b_0$. Define the product of two such tensors by concatenation and multiplication in $\mathcal C$ of the two adjacent old-arrow factors at the join. If either tensor has length zero this is simply the appropriate endpoint composition in $\mathcal C$. These formulas are separately multilinear in every factor, so repeated tensor lifting makes them well-defined bilinear compositions on $W$.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 28-30; explicit agent generalization and verification, not a locally archived proof.

proof.text: On a concatenation of three pure words, either order of composition multiplies the same old-arrow blocks in the same order. If two join points meet because the middle word has length zero, the equality is precisely associativity in $\mathcal C$. The old identities in $W_0(x,x)$ act as identities on both endpoints of every word. Pure-tensor generation in [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] extends these identities to all finite sums. There is therefore a graded category with the old object set and morphisms $W(x,y)$. Its inclusion of $\mathcal C$ is injective as graded modules by the projection to $W_0$. An arbitrary graded functor from $\mathcal C$ and graded linear map $E\to\mathcal D(Fs,Ft)$ extend uniquely by evaluating words: multiply their images in order. Existence again follows by tensor lifting; uniqueness follows because every tensor is such a product. In particular this is the free graded adjoining construction, with no further relations between different word lengths.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 28-30; explicit agent generalization and verification, not a locally archived proof.

proof.text: Take $E=Re$ in degree $n$. Set $D|_{\mathcal C}=d_{\mathcal C}$ and $D(e)=a$. On a homogeneous word $z_k\cdots z_1$ define $D$ as the sum of the terms obtained by replacing $z_j$ with $D(z_j)$, with coefficient $(-1)^{|z_k|+\cdots+|z_{j+1}|}$; if $z_j=e$, its replacement is the old arrow $a$ and the two adjacent old-arrow factors are composed. Each summand is multilinear, so [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] defines it on $W$. The formula respects old-arrow multiplication because $d_{\mathcal C}(bc)=d(b)c+(-1)^{|b|}bd(c)$: expanding the term at a merged factor gives exactly the two separate replacement terms, with these signs. It respects old units because $d(1)=0$. Partitioning the replacement positions between two concatenated words gives $D(vu)=D(v)u+(-1)^{|v|}vD(u)$. This verifies the derivation rule for the constructed composition.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 28-30; explicit agent generalization and verification, not a locally archived proof.

proof.text: Squaring this derivation on two homogeneous composable elements gives $D^2(vu)=D^2(v)u+vD^2(u)$: the two mixed terms have coefficients $(-1)^{|v|+1}$ and $(-1)^{|v|}$ and cancel. On old arrows $D^2=0$; on $e$ it is $d(a)=0$ by the closedness hypothesis. Induction on the number of factors in a word therefore gives $D^2=0$ on all pure words; their spanning property in [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] gives $D^2=0$ on all morphisms. Thus we have constructed a dg category. For a dg functor $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ and a degree-$n$ arrow $b:Fs\to Ft$ with $db=F(a)$, evaluation sending $e$ to $b$ commutes with $D$ on each word by the same replacement formula, and is the unique extension. This proves the required free dg adjoining universal property, including existence, and shows that its object set has not changed.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 28-30; explicit agent generalization and verification, not a locally archived proof.

proof.text: Let $F_mW(x,y)=\bigoplus_{0\leq r\leq m}W_r(x,y)$. The differential just constructed either preserves length (differentiating an old factor) or lowers it by one (replacing $e$ by $a$), so every $F_m$ is a subcomplex. Every element has finite word support, hence the filtration is exhaustive; $F_0=\mathcal C(x,y)$. The projection from $F_m$ to $F_{m-1}$ killing $W_m$ splits the inclusion as graded modules, and projection to $W_m$ identifies $F_m/F_{m-1}$ with $W_m$ as graded modules. In the quotient all replacement terms involving $a$ disappear. The remaining signed formula is exactly the tensor differential on the displayed tensor with $Re$ carrying zero differential, so the identification is an isomorphism of complexes. The tensor-product conventions and spanning property are those of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. This proves the entire filtration assertion without a flatness assumption or a splitting as complexes.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 28-30; explicit agent generalization and verification, not a locally archived proof.

proof.text: For a whole complex $V$, take $E$ to be its underlying graded module in steps 7-8 and prescribe $D(v)=d_V(v)$. The replacement formula of step 9 now preserves every word length. For homogeneous composable words $v,u$, expansion gives $D^2(vu)=D^2(v)u+((-1)^{|v|+1}+(-1)^{|v|})D(v)D(u)+vD^2(u)=D^2(v)u+vD^2(u)$. On each old factor $D^2=d_{\mathcal C}^2=0$, and on each new factor $D^2=d_V^2=0$; induction on the number of factors and linearity therefore give $D^2=0$ on every word and finite sum. The length-$m$ summand has exactly the tensor differential with $V$ in each new-arrow position. Word evaluation extends a dg functor from $\mathcal C$ precisely when the chosen map $V\to\mathcal D(Fs,Ft)$ is a chain map. Pure-tensor generation and lifting from [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] again give existence and uniqueness, so this direct sum is the free dg adjoining construction, as claimed. For the single-arrow construction, a morphism of attaching data is a dg functor $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal C^{\prime}$ taking $s,t,a$ to $s^{\prime},t^{\prime},a^{\prime}$ (with the same degree $n$); send $e$ to the new generator $e^{\prime}$. For the whole-complex construction it consists of a dg functor $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal C^{\prime}$ with $F(s)=s^{\prime}$ and $F(t)=t^{\prime}$, together with a chain map $h:V\to V^{\prime}$; send each new factor by $h$. In both cases send each old factor by $F$. Evaluation on words shows that these maps respect composition and the differential, preserve word length, and commute with the projections to the associated graded pieces; identities and composites agree on every factor and hence on every word. These are the asserted naturality statements.
